'''''Albuca bracteata''''' ([[synonym (taxonomy)|syn.]] ''Ornithogalum longebracteatum''<ref name="WCSP">{{Citation |contribution=Ornithogalum longebracteatum|title=World Checklist of Selected Plant Families |publisher=[[Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew]] |url=http://apps.kew.org/wcsp/namedetail.do?name_id=283613 |accessdate=2012-05-21}}</ref>), is known by the common names '''pregnant onion''',<ref name=hunt>[http://www.huntington.org/BotanicalDiv/ISI2006/isi/2006-28.html ''Ornithogalum longibracteatum'' Jacquin.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081027163420/http://www.huntington.org/BotanicalDiv/ISI2006/isi/2006-28.html |date=2008-10-27 }}  Plant Introductions of the Huntington Botanical Gardens.</ref> '''false sea onion''',<ref>{{cite book|last=Liepina|first=J.|title=False Sea Onion|publisher=Zvaigzne ABC|isbn=978-9984-40-610-7}}</ref> and '''sea-onion'''.<ref name=grin>{{GRIN | accessdate = 21 January 2018}}</ref> It is a species of [[bulb]]ous flowering plant in the family [[Asparagaceae]]. Its flowering stems can reach a height of 90 cm and can carry up to 100 greenish white flowers.

==Description==
Strap-shaped lanceolate leaves, 60 cm (2 ft) long and 2.5 cm (1 in) wide, protrude from a bulky bulb which is largely above ground. The roots are white and succulent. Many small, fragrant, white flowers, with a diameter of 0.5 cm and a green midvein, are located on [[raceme]]s that can reach 70–90 cm tall. Flowering usually occurs from spring through to early winter (May to August in the northern hemisphere), with 50 to 100 flowers per stalk.  One plant can have up to 300 flowers at one time. Fruit capsules are 10 mm long and 6 mm in diameter. Seeds are oblong with dimensions of 4 by 1.5 mm. ''Albuca bracteata'' is a cryptophyte, as the foliage dies back during drought periods.<ref name="The Encyclopedia of Succulents">{{cite web|last1=The Encyclopedia of Succulents|title=Albuca bracteata (Thunb.) J.C.Manning & Goldblatt|url=http://www.llifle.com/Encyclopedia/SUCCULENTS/Family/Hyacinthaceae/19749/Albuca_bracteata|publisher=Llifle Encyclopedia of living forms|accessdate=4 December 2017}}</ref><ref name="University of Connecticut"/>

==Taxonomy==
''Albuca bracteata'' was first described in 1794 by [[Carl Peter Thunberg]], as ''Ornithogalum bracteatum''.<ref name=WCSP_456152/> The specific epithet ''bracteatum'' refers to the [[bract]]s in the [[inflorescence]]; Thunberg described the species as "with longer flower bracts" ({{langx|la|bracteis floribus longioribus}}).<ref name=Thun94>{{Cite book |last1=Thunberg |first1=Carol. Pet. |date=1794 |title=Prodromus plantarum Capensium, volume 1 |volume=1 |url=https://biodiversitylibrary.org/page/3553182 |accessdate=2017-12-04 |page=62|language=la }}</ref> It was transferred to ''[[Albuca]]'' in 2009,<ref name=WCSP_456152/> along with other species of ''[[Ornithogalum]]'', based on a [[Molecular phylogenetics|molecular phylogenetic]] study.<ref name=MannForeDeveFay09>{{Cite journal |last1=Manning |first1=J.C. |last2=Forest |first2=F. |last3=Devey |first3=D.S. |last4=Fay |first4=M.F. |last5=Goldblatt |first5=P. |date=2009 |title=A molecular phylogeny and a revised classification of Ornithogaloideae (Hyacinthaceae) based on an analysis of four plastid DNA regions |journal=Taxon |volume=58 |pages=77–107 |name-list-style=amp |doi=10.1002/tax.581011 }}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
''Albuca bracteata'' is native to [[South Africa]] (the [[Cape Provinces]] and [[KwaZulu-Natal]]).<ref name=WCSP_456152/><ref name=grin/> It is also found in tropical east Africa, where it may be native<ref name=sanbi/> or introduced.<ref name=WCSP_456152/> It can be found growing in forests, forest margins, closed woodland and sheltered slopes.<ref name="South African National Biodiversity Institute">{{cite web|last1=South African National Biodiversity Institute|title=Pregnant Onion|url=http://redlist.sanbi.org/species.php?species=3795-156|website=Red List of South African Plants|accessdate=3 December 2017}}</ref> As of 2012, it had stable native populations with a conservation status of "least concern".<ref name="South African National Biodiversity Institute"/> It grows at altitudes of 0–300 m above sea level.<ref name="The Encyclopedia of Succulents"/>

==Cultivation==
''Albuca bracteata'' is primarily grown as a [[houseplant]].<ref name=hunt/> It is hardy to USDA zones of 9a-10b.<ref name="University of Connecticut">{{cite web|last1=University of Connecticut|title=Albuca bracteata (Thunb.) J.C.Manning & Goldblatt|url=http://florawww.eeb.uconn.edu/199500158.html|website=Biodiversity Education & Research Greenhouses|publisher=Unknown|accessdate=3 December 2017}}</ref> The ornamental value of this plant is based on the formation of bulblets. The common name "pregnant onion" is due to the small adventitious bulblets that form from the initial bulb scales, which are likened to "babies". It is frost tender, and requires light well drained soil,<ref name="Gardening Australia">{{cite web|last1=Gardening Australia|title=Plant Profile: Ornithogalum|url=http://www.abc.net.au/gardening/stories/s1866762.htm|website=ABC|accessdate=3 December 2017}}</ref> and bright light, although intense heat and light can scorch tissues.<ref name="The Encyclopedia of Succulents"/> Consistent watering is required for seed germination and survival.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Victorian Resources Online|title=Pregnant onion (Ornithogalum longebracteatum)|url=http://vro.agriculture.vic.gov.au/dpi/vro/vrosite.nsf/pages/weeds_pregnant-onion|website=Victorian Resources Online|publisher=Agriculture Victoria|accessdate=4 December 2017}}</ref> Mature plants will benefit from slight drying between waterings, although underwatering will induce dormancy. During the winter months this plant can be allowed to go dormant and the bulbs stored at cooler temperatures.<ref name="The Encyclopedia of Succulents"/>

===Propagation===
''Albuca bracteata'' can undergo vegetative and sexual reproduction. Propagation via bulblets is the most common method, whereby the bulblets are separated from the mother bulb and planted. Seed production provides genetic variation.  Micropropagation of ''Albuca bracteata'' has been achieved.<ref name="Ascough & Van Staden">{{cite journal|last1=Ascough|first1=G.D|last2=Van Staden|first2=J|title=Micropropagation of Albuca bracteata and A. nelsonii — Indigenous ornamentals with medicinal value|journal=South African Journal of Botany|date=August 2010| volume=76|issue=3|pages=579–584|doi=10.1016/j.sajb.2010.04.012|doi-access=free}}</ref> Bulblet production was found to be greatest ''in vitro'' between 10–30 °C, and was inhibited at 35 °C.<ref name="Ascough & Van Staden"/>

===Toxicity===
The sap can cause [[contact dermatitis]] and most parts of this plant are considered toxic to humans.<ref name="The Encyclopedia of Succulents"/> The bulb is a favoured dietary item of the [[Chacma baboon]].
